presentingComplaint: Sudden breathlessness and right-sided chest pain with a transient collapse
history: A 58-year-old man presented to the emergency department after a witnessed syncopal episode while walking to the bathroom that morning. For two days he had noticed progressive breathlessness and a sharp right-sided chest pain that was worse on deep inspiration. He returned four days ago from a 9-hour long-haul flight and had spent the preceding week largely immobile after a right knee arthroscopy. On the way to hospital he complained of central chest tightness radiating to the left arm, and the paramedic ECG showed anterior T-wave inversion, prompting a working diagnosis of acute coronary syndrome and administration of aspirin. He has hypertension on amlodipine, is an ex-smoker (20 pack-years), and has no prior cardiac history. He denies fever, cough or sputum. He noticed the right calf had become swollen and tender over the last three days.
examination: Alert but anxious and clammy, speaking in short sentences. Peripherally cool. Elevated JVP with a prominent 'a' wave and a loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound; a soft parasternal heave is palpable. Chest is clear to auscultation with no crepitations and equal air entry. Abdomen soft. Right calf is swollen with a 3.5 cm difference in circumference compared with the left, warm and tender along the deep venous line, with a positive Homans sign. No focal neurology.

labs.abg: pH 7.47, PaO2 8.1 kPa on room air, PaCO2 3.9 kPa, HCO3 22 (hypoxaemia with respiratory alkalosis)

imaging: ECG: sinus tachycardia with S1Q3T3 pattern, incomplete RBBB and T-wave inversion in V1-V4 (right precordial), no ST elevation. CTPA: large filling defects in the right main and lobar pulmonary arteries extending into segmental branches, with RV:LV diameter ratio 1.3, straightening of the interventricular septum and contrast reflux into the IVC, consistent with acute pulmonary embolism and right heart strain. Bedside echocardiography: dilated hypokinetic right ventricle with McConnell sign and TAPSE 14 mm; normal LV wall motion. Compression ultrasound of the right leg: non-compressible popliteal vein confirming proximal DVT.
microbiology: Not applicable - no infective focus; blood cultures not indicated.
differentialDiagnoses: Acute coronary syndrome (raised by anterior T-wave inversion, troponin elevation and radiating chest tightness - but coronary territory changes are explained by RV strain and normal LV on echo)
Acute aortic dissection (chest pain with hypotension - excluded by CTPA showing normal aorta and clear PA filling defects)
finalDiagnosis: Acute intermediate-high-risk pulmonary embolism with right ventricular strain, provoked by recent surgery, immobility and long-haul travel; concurrent troponin rise and anterior T-wave inversion mimic ACS.
citations: ESC - Acute Pulmonary Embolism (Diagnosis and Management) - 2019
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Deep Venous Thrombosis and Pulmonary Thromboembolism
stewardship: Non-infective diagnosis - no antimicrobials indicated. Antithrombotic stewardship applies: start therapeutic anticoagulation without delay while confirming the diagnosis (LMWH or a factor Xa inhibitor). This is intermediate-high risk (RV dysfunction plus troponin elevation) but not overt haemodynamic collapse, so systemic thrombolysis is NOT given up front - monitor on a high-dependency/ICU bed for haemodynamic deterioration and reserve reperfusion (systemic thrombolysis or catheter-directed therapy) for rescue if hypotension/shock develops. Avoid unnecessary antibiotics despite the acute febrile-appearing presentation.
contraindications: Systemic thrombolysis contraindicated if active bleeding, recent surgery (note recent knee arthroscopy - relative contraindication), recent stroke or intracranial pathology
Avoid DOACs in severe renal impairment (CrCl <15) and in significant hepatic impairment with coagulopathy
Do not delay anticoagulation waiting for CTPA when clinical probability is high and no bleeding risk
edgeCases: Troponin and anterior T-wave inversion misdirecting to ACS and cath lab activation, delaying anticoagulation
Hypotension progressing to obstructive shock, converting intermediate-high to high-risk PE requiring reperfusion
Syncope as the sole presenting feature of PE with minimal respiratory symptoms
expectedMaiK: Recognise acute PE with right ventricular strain (intermediate-high risk) despite an ACS-like ECG and troponin rise; confirm with CTPA, start immediate therapeutic anticoagulation, and monitor for haemodynamic deterioration rather than reflexively thrombolysing or treating as ACS.
expectedNextQuestions: Any recent surgery, immobilisation, long-haul travel, malignancy or prior VTE?
Is there unilateral leg swelling or calf pain suggesting DVT?
Any bleeding, recent stroke or contraindications to anticoagulation/thrombolysis?
Is the patient haemodynamically stable, or is systolic BP falling / lactate rising?
expectedInvestigations: Bedside transthoracic echocardiography for RV strain
regressionAssertions: Top diagnosis must be pe (pulmonary embolism), not acs despite anterior T-wave inversion and troponin rise
Management must include immediate therapeutic anticoagulation
Intermediate-high risk PE: systemic thrombolysis withheld up front, reserved for haemodynamic deterioration
CTPA must be listed as the confirmatory investigation
